blocks.title: Support and associated primes
blocks.body:
The support of an $A$-module $M$ is $\operatorname{Supp} M = \{\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Spec} A : M_{\mathfrak p} \ne 0\}$. A prime $\mathfrak p$ is associated to $M$ if $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(x)$ for some $x \in M$; the set of these is $\operatorname{Ass} M$. Guan and Hu use these notions without defining them (Mathlib already had them) and formalise, as their Lemma 2.1, the compatibility with localisation: for $A$ Noetherian and $M$ finitely generated,
$$\operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M) = \{\mathfrak p^e : \mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M,\ \mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing\},$$
that is, $\operatorname{Ass} M \cap \operatorname{Spec} S^{-1}A$.

blocks.title: Associated primes, regular sequences and flat base change
blocks.body: The preliminaries of Guan and Hu's formalisation of the Auslander-Buchsbaum-Serre criterion use three further facts about localisation: how associated primes behave under it (their Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2; the proof of their Proposition 3.2 uses that $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ is associated to $M_{\mathfrak p}$ when $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M$), that a regular sequence inside a prime $\mathfrak p$ stays regular in $A_{\mathfrak p}$ (their §2.4 and Proposition 4.6), and how this relates to base change: they formalise that weakly regular sequences survive flat base change and regular sequences survive faithfully flat base change, and add separate lemmas for localisation. Since $A \to A_{\mathfrak p}$ is flat but usually not faithfully flat, the second result does not apply to it, and the hypothesis that the sequence lies in $\mathfrak p$ takes its place. This section proves the first two facts and the statement about faithful flatness. Recall that $\operatorname{Ass} M$ is the set of primes of the form $\operatorname{Ann}(x)$ with $x \in M$.

blocks.title: Associated primes exist
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be Noetherian and $M 
e 0$ an $A$-module. Every ideal that is maximal in the set $\{\operatorname{Ann}(x) : x \in M,\ x 
e 0\}$ is prime. Consequently $\operatorname{Ass} M 
e \varnothing$, and every zero-divisor on $M$ (an $a$ with $ay = 0$ for some $y 
e 0$) lies in some associated prime of $M$.

The set is nonempty because $M 
e 0$, so it has a maximal element, $A$ being Noetherian (every nonempty set of ideals of a Noetherian ring has a maximal element; see [[noetherian-rings]]). Let $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(x)$ be maximal. It is proper since $x 
e 0$. Let $ab \in \mathfrak p$ with $b 
otin \mathfrak p$. Then $bx 
e 0$ and $\operatorname{Ann}(bx) \supseteq \operatorname{Ann}(x) = \mathfrak p$, so by maximality $\operatorname{Ann}(bx) = \mathfrak p$. Since $a(bx) = (ab)x = 0$, we get $a \in \mathfrak p$. So $\mathfrak p$ is prime and lies in $\operatorname{Ass} M$.

If $ay = 0$ with $y 
e 0$, the annihilators $\operatorname{Ann}(z)$, $z 
e 0$, that contain $\operatorname{Ann}(y)$ form a nonempty set; take a maximal one. Any annihilator of a nonzero element containing it also contains $\operatorname{Ann}(y)$, so it is maximal in the whole set, hence an associated prime, and it contains $a$. (The note [brownass] proves the first part this way; the Stacks Project, Lemmas 10.63.7 and 10.63.9, reaches the same statements through filtrations with quotients $A/\mathfrak p_i$.)

blocks.title: Associated primes and localisation
blocks.body:
Let $S \subseteq A$ be multiplicative and $M$ an $A$-module.

1. If $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M$ and $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$, then $S^{-1}\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M)$.
2. If $A$ is Noetherian, every associated prime of $S^{-1}M$ arises in this way:
$$\operatorname{Ass}_{S^{-1}A}(S^{-1}M) = \{S^{-1}\mathfrak p : \mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M,\ \mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing\}.$$
This is Stacks Lemma 10.63.16; Guan-Hu Lemma 2.1 states it for finitely generated $M$.
3. If $A$ is Noetherian and $M$ is finitely generated, every prime minimal over $\operatorname{Ann} M$ is associated to $M$ (Guan-Hu Lemma 2.2; Stacks Lemma 10.63.8 for minimal primes of the support).

In particular, taking $S = A \setminus \mathfrak p$ in part 1: if $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Ass} M$ then the maximal ideal $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ is associated to $M_{\mathfrak p}$, which is the step used in Guan-Hu Proposition 3.2.

1. Let $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(x)$. We show $\operatorname{Ann}_{S^{-1}A}(x/1) = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. If $a \in \mathfrak p$ then $(a/s)(x/1) = ax/s = 0$. Conversely, if $(a/s)(x/1) = 0$, then $uax = 0$ for some $u \in S$, so $ua \in \mathfrak p$; since $u \notin \mathfrak p$ and $\mathfrak p$ is prime, $a \in \mathfrak p$ and $a/s \in S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. The ideal $S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ is prime by the correspondence theorem (in particular proper, so $x/1 \ne 0$).

2. Let $Q = \operatorname{Ann}(x/s)$ be a prime of $S^{-1}A$ and $\mathfrak p = Q \cap A$ its contraction, a prime disjoint from $S$ with $Q = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. As $A$ is Noetherian, $\mathfrak p = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$. Each $(a_i/1)(x/s) = 0$, so $u_ia_ix = 0$ for some $u_i \in S$. Put $u = u_1\cdots u_n$ and $y = ux$. Then $a_iy = 0$ for all $i$, so $\mathfrak p \subseteq \operatorname{Ann}(y)$. Conversely, if $by = 0$ then $(b/1)(x/s) = bx/s = bux/(us) = by/(us) = 0$, so $b/1 \in Q$ and $b \in \mathfrak p$. Thus $\mathfrak p = \operatorname{Ann}(y) \in \operatorname{Ass} M$, and $Q = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$. Together with part 1 this gives the equality.

3. Let $\mathfrak p$ be minimal over $\operatorname{Ann} M$. By the support theorem, $\mathfrak p \in V(\operatorname{Ann} M) = \operatorname{Supp} M$, so $M_{\mathfrak p} \ne 0$. The ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is Noetherian, so by the existence theorem $M_{\mathfrak p}$ has an associated prime, and by part 2 it is $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p}$ for some $\mathfrak q \in \operatorname{Ass} M$ with $\mathfrak q \subseteq \mathfrak p$. Being the annihilator of an element of $M$, $\mathfrak q$ contains $\operatorname{Ann} M$; by minimality of $\mathfrak p$, $\mathfrak q = \mathfrak p$. This is Guan and Hu's argument: localise at the minimal prime and use that the localisation has only one prime containing the annihilator.

blocks.title: Associated primes of Z/12 and its localisations
blocks.body: Let $M = \mathbb Z/12$ as a $\mathbb Z$-module. Find $\operatorname{Ass} M$, then $\operatorname{Ass}$ of $M_{(2)}$, of $M_{(5)}$ and of $M[1/2] = S^{-1}M$ for $S = \{2^n\}$, and compare with part 3 of the theorem.
blocks.solution:
The annihilator of the class of $x \ne 0$ is $(12/\gcd(x, 12))\mathbb Z$, so the annihilators of nonzero elements are $12\mathbb Z, 6\mathbb Z, 4\mathbb Z, 3\mathbb Z, 2\mathbb Z$ (for $\gcd = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6$). The prime ones are $2\mathbb Z = \operatorname{Ann}(6)$ and $3\mathbb Z = \operatorname{Ann}(4) = \operatorname{Ann}(8)$. So $\operatorname{Ass} M = \{(2), (3)\}$. Also $\operatorname{Ann} M = 12\mathbb Z$, whose minimal primes $(2)$ and $(3)$ are both associated, as part 3 predicts; the maximal annihilators $2\mathbb Z, 3\mathbb Z$ are the primes of the existence theorem.

At $(2)$: of the two associated primes only $(2)$ is disjoint from $\mathbb Z \setminus (2)$, so $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(2)} = \{2\mathbb Z_{(2)}\}$. This matches the direct computation $M_{(2)} \cong \mathbb Z/4$ (the $3$-part dies because $3$ is inverted), where $\operatorname{Ann}(2) = 2\mathbb Z_{(2)}$.

At $(5)$: neither associated prime is contained in $(5)$, so $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(5)} = \varnothing$; indeed $M_{(5)} = 0$ because $12$ is a unit of $\mathbb Z_{(5)}$ that kills $M$, consistent with the existence theorem.

For $S = \{2^n\}$: $(2)$ meets $S$ and $(3)$ does not, so $\operatorname{Ass} S^{-1}M = \{3\mathbb Z[1/2]\}$, and indeed $S^{-1}M \cong \mathbb Z/3$ (the $\mathbb Z/4$ part is killed by $4 \in S$).

blocks.title: Regular sequences under localisation
blocks.body:
Following Stacks Definition 10.68.1, $x_1, \dots, x_r \in A$ is an $M$-regular sequence if each $x_i$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/(x_1, \dots, x_{i-1})M$ and $M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M \ne 0$. Let $x_1, \dots, x_r$ be $M$-regular and $S \subseteq A$ multiplicative.

1. Each $x_i/1$ is a non-zero-divisor on $S^{-1}M/(x_1/1, \dots, x_{i-1}/1)S^{-1}M$. Hence $x_1/1, \dots, x_r/1$ is $S^{-1}M$-regular as soon as $S^{-1}M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)S^{-1}M \ne 0$.
2. If $M$ is finitely generated, $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Supp} M$ and all $x_i \in \mathfrak p$, then $x_1/1, \dots, x_r/1$ is an $M_{\mathfrak p}$-regular sequence in $A_{\mathfrak p}$.

Part 2 is the step behind Guan-Hu Proposition 4.6, $\operatorname{depth}_{\mathfrak p} M \le \operatorname{depth} M_{\mathfrak p}$. The definition asks for $M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M \ne 0$ and does not ask the $x_i$ to lie in a maximal ideal; for a finitely generated module over a local ring the two conditions agree, by Nakayama's lemma. Guan and Hu's Lean code separates the two parts: a weakly regular sequence (IsWeaklyRegular) satisfies only the non-zero-divisor conditions, which part 1 shows survive any localisation, and a regular one (IsRegular) also has the nonvanishing condition, which is the part that needs $x_i \in \mathfrak p$.

Write $I_i = (x_1, \dots, x_i)$. For any ideal $I$ we have $S^{-1}(IM) = (S^{-1}I)(S^{-1}M)$: an element $(\sum_j a_jm_j)/s$ with $a_j \in I$ equals $\sum_j (a_j/1)(m_j/s)$, and conversely $(a/t)(m/s) = am/(ts)$. Since localisation is exact, $S^{-1}(M/I_{i-1}M) \cong S^{-1}M/(S^{-1}I_{i-1})S^{-1}M$, and $S^{-1}I_{i-1}$ is generated by $x_1/1, \dots, x_{i-1}/1$.

1. Multiplication by $x_i$ is injective on $N = M/I_{i-1}M$, i.e. $0 \to N \xrightarrow{x_i} N$ is exact. Localising preserves exactness, and $S^{-1}$ of multiplication by $x_i$ is multiplication by $x_i/1$; so $x_i/1$ is injective on $S^{-1}N$, which is the module in the statement by the first paragraph.

2. By part 1 only the last condition needs proof. $M_{\mathfrak p}$ is a finitely generated module over the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$, and it is nonzero because $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Supp} M$. Since all $x_i/1$ lie in $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$, we have $(x_1, \dots, x_r)M_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq \mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}M_{\mathfrak p}$, and Nakayama's lemma gives $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}M_{\mathfrak p} \ne M_{\mathfrak p}$. Hence $M_{\mathfrak p}/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M_{\mathfrak p} \ne 0$.

The hypothesis $x_i \in \mathfrak p$ cannot be dropped: $2$ is a $\mathbb Z$-regular sequence, but in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$ it is a unit and $\mathbb Z_{(3)}/2\mathbb Z_{(3)} = 0$.

blocks.title: A sequence that becomes regular after localising
blocks.body: In $A = k[x, y, z]$ ($k$ a field) the Stacks Project (Example 10.68.2) notes that $x, y(1-x), z(1-x)$ is $A$-regular while $y(1-x), z(1-x), x$ is not. Verify the second claim, and show that $y(1-x), z(1-x), x$ is regular in $A_{\mathfrak m}$ for $\mathfrak m = (x, y, z)$.
blocks.solution:
In $A/(y(1-x))$ the class of $y$ is nonzero: $y = y(1-x)g$ would force $(1-x)g = 1$, impossible by degrees. But $z(1-x)\cdot y = z\cdot y(1-x) \in (y(1-x))$. So $z(1-x)$ is a zero-divisor on $A/(y(1-x))$ and the sequence is not regular.

In $A_{\mathfrak m}$ the element $1 - x \notin \mathfrak m$ is a unit. Hence $(y(1-x)) = (y)$ and $(y(1-x), z(1-x)) = (y, z)$ as ideals of $A_{\mathfrak m}$, and multiplying an element by a unit does not change whether it is a non-zero-divisor on a module. So $y(1-x), z(1-x), x$ is $A_{\mathfrak m}$-regular if and only if $y, z, x$ is. Now $y, z, x$ is $A$-regular: $A/(y) \cong k[x, z]$, on which $z$ is a non-zero-divisor; $A/(y, z) \cong k[x]$, on which $x$ is a non-zero-divisor; and $A/(y, z, x) \cong k \ne 0$. All three lie in $\mathfrak m$, $A$ is finitely generated over itself and $\mathfrak m \in \operatorname{Supp} A$, so part 2 of the theorem shows that $y, z, x$ is $A_{\mathfrak m}$-regular. (Stacks Lemma 10.68.4 explains the general phenomenon: over a Noetherian local ring every permutation of a regular sequence of a finitely generated module is regular.)

blocks.title: Localisation is flat but rarely faithfully flat

blocks.body:
$S^{-1}A$ is flat over $A$ because localisation is exact and $S^{-1}N \cong N \otimes_A S^{-1}A$. So (1) and (2) are equivalent by Stacks Lemma 10.39.16.

(2) implies (4): the image of $\operatorname{Spec} S^{-1}A$ is the set of primes disjoint from $S$. If some $s \in S$ were not a unit, it would lie in a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, which meets $S$ and so is not in the image.

(3) implies (4): if $s \in S$ is not a unit, then $N = A/sA \ne 0$, but $S^{-1}N = 0$, because for $n \in N$ and $t \in S$ we have $n/t = sn/(st) = 0$, as $sn = 0$ in $N$.

(4) implies (1), (2), (3): if $S$ consists of units then $\iota\colon A \to S^{-1}A$ satisfies Strickland's conditions with $B = A$ and the identity map (every $a/s$ equals $\iota(as^{-1})$, and $sa = 0$ forces $a = 0$), so $\iota$ is an isomorphism, and an isomorphism has all three properties.

For the last sentence, $A \setminus \mathfrak p$ consists of units exactly when every non-unit lies in $\mathfrak p$, i.e. when $\mathfrak p$ is the unique maximal ideal.

- An $M$-regular sequence need not stay regular in $A_{\mathfrak p}$ if some $x_i \notin \mathfrak p$: the quotient can become zero. Conversely, a sequence can be regular in some $A_{\mathfrak m}$ without being regular in $A$ (the example above, at $\mathfrak m = (x, y, z)$). Each single condition "$x_i$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M/I_{i-1}M$" is a local property, since it says that a kernel vanishes, so the failure in $A$ must show up at some other maximal ideal: in the example, at one containing $1 - x$, where $x$ becomes a unit.
- Over a local ring with $M$ finitely generated, some texts require the elements of a regular sequence to lie in the maximal ideal, while the Stacks Project requires $M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M \ne 0$; by Nakayama's lemma these agree. Over a non-local ring only the second condition makes sense, and it is the condition that can be lost on localising.
- Flatness of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ lets one push exact sequences and regular sequences forward, but faithful flatness, which would let one pull properties back from $A_{\mathfrak p}$ to $A$, fails unless $A$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p$. Properties of $A$ are recovered from all localisations together, by the local-global principle of the next section; this is why Guan and Hu's result for faithfully flat base change does not cover $R \to R_{\mathfrak p}$, and why they add separate lemmas for localisation.

1. (Basic) Find $\operatorname{Ass}_{\mathbb Z}(\mathbb Z/360)$, and use the localisation theorem to find the associated primes of $(\mathbb Z/360)_{(3)}$ and of $S^{-1}(\mathbb Z/360)$ for $S = \{5^n\}$.
2. (Basic) Let $A$ be Noetherian and $M \ne 0$. Show that the set of zero-divisors on $M$ is exactly the union of the associated primes of $M$.
3. (Medium) Let $A = k[x, y]$ and $M = A/(x^2, xy)$. Show that $\operatorname{Ass} M = \{(x), (x, y)\}$ (find elements with these annihilators and show there are no others), and compute $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(x)}$ and $\operatorname{Ass} M_{(x,y)}$.
4. (Medium) Let $A$ be Noetherian and $M$ any $A$-module. Show that $\mathfrak p \in \operatorname{Supp} M$ if and only if some associated prime of $M$ is contained in $\mathfrak p$.
5. (Harder) Show that $x \in A$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M$ if and only if $x/1$ is a non-zero-divisor on $M_{\mathfrak m}$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and deduce that for $M$ finitely generated over a Noetherian ring, a sequence $x_1, \dots, x_r$ with $M/(x_1, \dots, x_r)M \ne 0$ is $M$-regular if and only if, for every maximal $\mathfrak m$, its image satisfies the non-zero-divisor conditions on $M_{\mathfrak m}$.

checks.claim: Ass_Z(Z/12) = {(2),(3)}; Ass_Z(Z/360) = {(2),(3),(5)}; (Z/12)_(2) has 4 elements, (Z/12)_(5) = 0, (Z/12)[1/2] has 3 elements; annihilators of nonzero elements of Z/12 are 12,6,4,3,2
checks.python:
from math import gcd
def isprime(n): return n > 1 and all(n % d for d in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1))
def ann_gens(n): return sorted({n // gcd(x, n) for x in range(1, n)})
assert ann_gens(12) == [2, 3, 4, 6, 12]
def ass(n): return sorted(g for g in ann_gens(n) if isprime(g))
assert ass(12) == [2, 3] and ass(360) == [2, 3, 5]
assert 12 // gcd(6, 12) == 2 and 12 // gcd(4, 12) == 3 and 12 // gcd(8, 12) == 3
def loc_classes(n, S):
    S = sorted(set(x % n for x in S))
    pairs = [(a, s) for a in range(n) for s in S]
    classes = []
    for p in pairs:
        for c in classes:
            (a, s), (b, t) = p, c[0]
            if any((u * (a * t - b * s)) % n == 0 for u in S): c.append(p); break
        else: classes.append([p])
    return classes
odd = [x for x in range(12) if x % 2]            # residues of the integers outside (2)
assert len(loc_classes(12, odd)) == 4             # (Z/12)_(2) = Z/4
not5 = sorted({m % 12 for m in range(1, 200) if m % 5})   # residues of integers outside (5); 12 gives 0
assert 0 in not5 and len(loc_classes(12, not5)) == 1      # (Z/12)_(5) = 0
assert len(loc_classes(12, [1, 2, 4, 8])) == 3   # Z/12[1/2] = Z/3
# localisation of Ass at (3) and at powers of 5 for Z/360 (exercise data): primes contained in (3) / disjoint from 5^n
assert [p for p in ass(360) if p == 3] == [3] and [p for p in ass(360) if p != 5] == [2, 3]

blocks.title: Arithmetic: discrete valuation rings and Dedekind domains
blocks.body: In number theory localisation is used to make ideal theory simple. The ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$ of a number field may lack unique factorisation (see [[ideals]]), but each localisation $\mathcal O_{K,\mathfrak p}$ at a nonzero prime is a discrete valuation ring, a ring whose ideals are just the powers of one prime element. Global information is recovered because a domain is the intersection of its localisations. Sutherland's lecture develops exactly this, and Coykendall and Kettinger study class groups of the rings $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ obtained by inverting one element.

blocks.title: Discrete valuation ring
blocks.body: A discrete valuation on a field $K$ is a surjective map $v\colon K^\times \to \mathbb Z$ with $v(xy) = v(x) + v(y)$ and $v(x + y) \ge \min(v(x), v(y))$ (when $x + y \ne 0$). Its valuation ring $R = \{x \in K^\times : v(x) \ge 0\} \cup \{0\}$ is a discrete valuation ring (DVR). An element $\pi$ with $v(\pi) = 1$ is a uniformiser. A DVR is a local principal ideal domain: its units are the elements of valuation $0$, its maximal ideal is $\pi R$, and every nonzero ideal is $\pi^kR$ for a unique $k \ge 0$. For a Noetherian local domain of dimension one, being a DVR is equivalent to being integrally closed, and also to the maximal ideal being principal (Stacks Lemma 10.119.7, which lists further equivalent conditions).

blocks.title: Localising the integers at a prime
blocks.body: Show that $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ is the valuation ring of the $p$-adic valuation $v_p$ on $\mathbb Q$, find its units and ideals, and its residue field. Do the same for $k[x]_{(x-2)}$.
blocks.solution:
Write a nonzero rational as $x = p^k a/b$ with $p 
mid ab$; then $v_p(x) = k$ is well defined, additive under products, and $v_p(x + y) \ge \min(v_p(x), v_p(y))$ (factor out the smaller power of $p$). $x \in \mathbb Z_{(p)}$ iff it has a representative with denominator prime to $p$ iff $k \ge 0$. Units: $v_p(x) = 0$, i.e. $x = a/b$ with $p 
mid ab$. Every nonzero $x \in \mathbb Z_{(p)}$ is $p^{v_p(x)}u$ with $u$ a unit, so an ideal $I 
e 0$ equals $p^k\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ with $k$ the least valuation in $I$; here $\pi = p$. The residue field is $\mathbb Z_{(p)}/p\mathbb Z_{(p)} \cong \operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb Z/p) = \mathbb F_p$, as in the theorem on the local ring at a prime.

For $k[x]_{(x-2)}$, the rational functions defined at $2$, the valuation is the order of vanishing at $2$, the uniformiser is $x - 2$, the maximal ideal is the set of functions vanishing at $2$, and the residue field is $k$, via evaluation at $2$ (Sutherland, Example 2.4).

blocks.title: Dedekind domains are locally DVRs
blocks.body: For a Noetherian domain $A$ the following are equivalent: (i) $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a DVR for every nonzero prime $\mathfrak p$; (ii) $A$ is integrally closed and $\dim A \le 1$. Such $A$ is a Dedekind domain. Every PID, in particular $\mathbb Z$ and $k[x]$, is a Dedekind domain.

(ii) implies (i): $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Noetherian local domain, integrally closed by part 2 of the preservation theorem, and of dimension $1$ (its primes are $0$ and $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$). By the characterisation of DVRs among Noetherian local domains of dimension one (Stacks Lemma 10.119.7; Sutherland quotes the same fact from his first lecture in the proof of his Proposition 2.9), it is a DVR.

(i) implies (ii): a DVR is integrally closed (if $x \notin R$ then $v(x) < 0$, and in a monic equation $x^n + a_1x^{n-1} + \dots + a_n = 0$ the term $x^n$ has strictly smaller valuation than all the others, which is impossible), so by the intersection theorem $A = \bigcap A_{\mathfrak p}$ is an intersection of integrally closed rings with the same fraction field, hence integrally closed. If $0 \ne \mathfrak q \subsetneq \mathfrak p$ were a chain of primes in $A$, then $A_{\mathfrak p}$ would have the chain $0 \subsetneq \mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p} \subsetneq \mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$, but a DVR has only two primes. For a PID, each $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a local PID that is not a field, which is a DVR (the valuation is the exponent of a generator of $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$).

blocks.title: A non-principal prime becomes principal locally
blocks.body: In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ let $P_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$, the prime with $P_2^2 = (2)$ from [[ideals]]. Show that $P_2D_{P_2}$ is generated by $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, so $D_{P_2}$ is a DVR with uniformiser $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, although $P_2$ is not principal in $D$.
blocks.solution:
In $D_{P_2}$ the element $3$ is a unit, since $3 \notin P_2$ (elements of $P_2$ are $a + b\sqrt{-5}$ with $a \equiv b \pmod 2$). Now $(1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}) = 1 + 5 = 6$, so
$$2 = \frac{(1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})}{3} \in (1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2}.$$
Hence $P_2D_{P_2} = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2} = (1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2}$. The local ring is a DVR because $D$ is a Dedekind domain. The valuation of $2$ is $2$ (as $(2) = P_2^2$) and that of $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ is $1$ (as $(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = P_2P_3$ with $P_3 = (3, 1+\sqrt{-5}) \ne P_2$). Locally at $P_2$ the failure of unique factorisation is invisible: it is a global phenomenon, measured by the class group.

blocks.title: Class groups of localisations (Claborn)
blocks.body:
Let $D$ be a Dedekind domain and $\alpha \in D$ a nonzero non-unit with $(\alpha) = \mathfrak p_1^{n_1}\cdots\mathfrak p_k^{n_k}$. Then
$$\operatorname{Cl}(D[1/\alpha]) \cong \operatorname{Cl}(D)/\langle[\mathfrak p_1], \dots, [\mathfrak p_k]\rangle .$$
This is Theorem 4.1 of Coykendall-Kettinger, a special case of a theorem of Claborn; the proof is not given here (see [coyk] §4 and the references there). Their Theorem 4.2 states that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ is the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$ in $K$; read it with care, because the integral closure is $\mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$, which contains $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ and can be strictly larger (see the example 'Inverting an element versus inverting its norm' below; equality holds for instance when $\alpha \in \mathbb Z$, which covers the rings $\mathcal O_K[1/n]$ of their Theorem 4.5; their Corollary 4.4 applies Theorem 4.1 to $N(\alpha)$ directly and does not depend on Theorem 4.2). They also use (Proposition 5.2, due to Gilmer) that every ring between a Dedekind domain $D$ and its fraction field is an intersection of localisations $D_{\mathfrak p}$.

blocks.title: Inverting 2 in Z[sqrt(-5)]
blocks.body: Using the theorem, compute $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}][1/2])$, and verify by hand that the non-principal prime $P_3' = (3, 1 - \sqrt{-5})$ becomes principal in $D[1/2]$.
blocks.solution:
(This is our application of their Theorem 4.1; the paper's own examples invert other elements.) $\operatorname{Cl}(D) \cong \mathbb Z/2$, generated by the class of the non-principal prime $P_2$ (see [[class-group]]). Since $(2) = P_2^2$, the theorem gives $\operatorname{Cl}(D[1/2]) \cong \operatorname{Cl}(D)/\langle [P_2] \rangle = 0$: the ring $D[1/2]$ is a PID.

By hand: in $D$ we have $P_2P_3' = (1 - \sqrt{-5})$ (an exercise on [[ideals]], checked below). Extension is multiplicative, $(IJ)^e = I^eJ^e$, and $P_2^e = D[1/2]$ because $2 \in P_2$ is a unit of $D[1/2]$. So
$$P_3'D[1/2] = P_2^eP_3'^e = (P_2P_3')^e = (1 - \sqrt{-5})D[1/2].$$

blocks.title: A localisation is the intersection of its local rings
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain with fraction field $K$ and $S$ multiplicative with $0 
otin S$. Inside $K$,
$$S^{-1}A =  igcap_{\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing} A_{\mathfrak p},$$
the intersection over primes of $A$ disjoint from $S$; and for a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$, $\mathfrak pS^{-1}A 
e S^{-1}A$ if and only if $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$. For a Dedekind domain $D$ and $R = S^{-1}D$ this is the formula $R =  igcap_{\mathfrak pR 
e R} D_{\mathfrak p}$ that Coykendall and Kettinger quote from Gilmer for every ring between $D$ and $K$ (their Proposition 5.2). They use it in proving Theorems 5.3, 5.5 and 5.8; in Theorem 5.5 the overring in question is $D[1/a]$, so the case proved here is the one needed there.

The second statement is part 3 of the extension-contraction theorem. For the first, put $B = S^{-1}A \subseteq K$, a domain with fraction field $K$. By the theorem that a domain is the intersection of its localisations, $B =  igcap_Q B_Q$ over the primes $Q$ of $B$, and these are the $Q = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$. It remains to see $B_Q = A_{\mathfrak p}$ as subrings of $K$. If $t \in A \setminus \mathfrak p$ then $t/1 
otin Q$, so $A_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq B_Q$. Conversely an element of $B_Q$ is $b/c$ with $b = a/s$, $c = a'/s'$, $a, a' \in A$, $s, s' \in S$ and $c 
otin Q$; then $a' 
otin \mathfrak p$ (otherwise $c = a'/s' \in Q$), and $b/c = (as')/(sa')$ with $sa' 
otin \mathfrak p$ because $s 
otin \mathfrak p$. So $b/c \in A_{\mathfrak p}$.

blocks.title: Inverting an element versus inverting its norm
blocks.body: Let $K = \mathbb Q(i)$, $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[i]$ and $\alpha = 2 + i$, so $N(\alpha) = 5$. Is $R = \mathbb Z[i][1/\alpha]$ the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/5]$ in $K$? Then describe in general, for a number field $K$ and nonzero $\alpha \in \mathcal O_K$, how $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ and $\mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$ compare.
blocks.solution:
By the theorem on what localisation preserves (part 2, with $A = \mathbb Z$, $B = K$, $B' = \mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[i]$ and $S = \{5^n\}$, noting $S^{-1}K = K$), the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/5]$ in $K$ is $\mathbb Z[i][1/5]$. It contains $R$, since $1/(2+i) = (2-i)/5$. But it is strictly larger. In the PID $\mathbb Z[i]$ we have $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$, and $2 - i$ is a Gaussian prime (its norm $5$ is prime) that is not an associate of $2+i$ (the associates of $2+i$ are $\pm(2+i)$ and $\pm(1-2i)$). By unique factorisation no power $(2+i)^n$ is divisible by $2 - i$, so the prime $(2-i)$ is disjoint from $\{(2+i)^n\}$ and extends to a proper prime of $R$ containing $5$. Thus $5$ is not a unit of $R$: $1/5 \notin R$, and $R$ does not even contain $\mathbb Z[1/5]$.

In general, let $N(\alpha)$ be the product of the conjugates of $\alpha$ and $\beta = N(\alpha)/\alpha$, the product of the conjugates other than $\alpha$ itself. Then $\beta \in K$ and $\beta$ is an algebraic integer, so $\beta \in \mathcal O_K$, and $1/\alpha = \beta/N(\alpha)$. Hence always $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha] \subseteq \mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$, the latter being the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$ in $K$. Equality holds if and only if $N(\alpha)$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$, that is (by the description of the saturation of $\{\alpha^n\}$ as the complement of the union of the primes not containing $\alpha$) if and only if every prime of $\mathcal O_K$ containing $N(\alpha)$ contains $\alpha$. For $\alpha \in \mathbb Z$ this holds, since then $N(\alpha) = \alpha^{[K:\mathbb Q]}$; for $\alpha = 2 + i$ it fails at the prime $(2 - i)$. Coykendall and Kettinger's proof of their Theorem 4.2 shows correctly that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ is integrally closed and that $1/\alpha$ is integral over $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$; what it needs in addition, and what fails here, is that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ contain $1/N(\alpha)$.

blocks.title: Conjugation and localisation
blocks.body: Coykendall and Kettinger (Example 5.1, Theorem 5.8) ask when a Galois automorphism $\sigma$ preserves an overring of $\mathcal O_K$. Let $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, $\sigma$ complex conjugation and $\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{-5}$. Show that $\sigma(D_{\mathfrak p}) = D_{\sigma(\mathfrak p)}$ for every prime $\mathfrak p$, but that $R = D[1/\alpha]$ satisfies $\sigma(R) \ne R$.
blocks.solution:
$\sigma$ is a ring automorphism of $D$, extended to $K = \operatorname{Frac} D$ by $\sigma(a/s) = \sigma(a)/\sigma(s)$. It maps $D \setminus \mathfrak p$ bijectively onto $D \setminus \sigma(\mathfrak p)$, so $\sigma(D_{\mathfrak p}) = \{\sigma(a)/\sigma(s) : s 
otin \mathfrak p\} = D_{\sigma(\mathfrak p)}$. Likewise $\sigma(R) = D[1/\sigma(\alpha)] = D[1/(1 - \sqrt{-5})]$.

So $\sigma(R) \subseteq R$ would require $1 - \sqrt{-5}$ to be a unit of $R$, i.e. to lie in no prime of $D$ disjoint from $\{\alpha^n\}$ (the saturation criterion). Consider $\chi\colon D 	o \mathbb F_3$, $a + b\sqrt{-5} \mapsto a + b  mod 3$. It is a ring map because $(\sqrt{-5})^2 = -5 \equiv 1 = 1^2 \pmod 3$. Its kernel $P_3'$ contains $3$ and $1 - \sqrt{-5}$, and conversely $a + b\sqrt{-5} = (a + b) - b(1 - \sqrt{-5})$ lies in $(3, 1 - \sqrt{-5})$ when $3 \mid a + b$; so $P_3' = (3, 1 - \sqrt{-5})$, a prime with residue field $\mathbb F_3$. Since $\chi(\alpha) = 2 
e 0$, $P_3'$ contains no power of $\alpha$, so $P_3'R$ is a proper prime of $R$ containing $1 - \sqrt{-5}$. Hence $1/(1 - \sqrt{-5}) = \sigma(1/\alpha) 
otin R$ and $\sigma(R) 
e R$. This is the paper's observation that $ rac{1}{\alpha}\sigma( rac{1}{\alpha}) =  rac16 
otin R$ (indeed $6 \in P_3'$). In the language of their Theorem 5.8: $P_3 = \sigma(P_3') = (3, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$ satisfies $P_3R = R$ since it contains $\alpha$, while $\sigma(P_3)R = P_3'R 
e R$.

blocks.body:
1. (Basic) Show that $\mathbb Z[i][1/(1+i)] = \mathbb Z[i][1/2]$, using $2 = -i(1+i)^2$, and check it against the criterion in the example on norms.
2. (Medium) Let $K$ be a number field and $n \in \mathbb Z$ nonzero. Show that $\mathcal O_K[1/n]$ is the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/n]$ in $K$ and that $\sigma(\mathcal O_K[1/n]) = \mathcal O_K[1/n]$ for every automorphism $\sigma$ of $K$.
3. (Medium) In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ list the primes $\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak pD[1/6] = D[1/6]$, and show that $D[1/6] = \bigcap D_{\mathfrak p}$ over the remaining primes.
4. (Harder) With $D$ and $\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{-5}$ as in the conjugation example, show that $D[1/\alpha] \cap D[1/\sigma(\alpha)]$ is not $D$: describe it as $\bigcap D_{\mathfrak p}$ over an explicit set of primes, and identify it as $D[1/2]$. (Use $(\alpha) = P_2P_3$ and $(\sigma(\alpha)) = P_2P_3'$.)

1. (Basic) Show that the only DVR with fraction field $\mathbb Q$ containing $\mathbb Z$ and with residue characteristic $p$ is $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$.
2. (Basic) Show that $\mathbb Z[1/6]$ is a Dedekind domain and a PID, and list its maximal ideals.
3. (Medium) Show that $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ is not integrally closed, and that its localisation at the prime $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-3})$ is not a DVR, while its localisation at every other nonzero prime is.
4. (Medium) Use Claborn's theorem to show that for every Dedekind domain $D$ with finite class group there is $\alpha$ with $D[1/\alpha]$ a PID.
5. (Harder) Prove the first half of Gilmer's statement in the simplest case: every ring $R$ with $\mathbb Z \subseteq R \subseteq \mathbb Q$ equals $\mathbb Z[1/p : p \in P]$ for a set of primes $P$, and is the intersection of the $\mathbb Z_{(q)}$ for $q \notin P$.

checks.claim: Z[sqrt(-5)]: (1+w)(1-w) = 6; P2^2 = (2); P2 * P3' = (1 - w); 3 not in P2 (lattice HNF computation of ideals)
checks.python:
from math import gcd
def mul(p, q):  # (a + b w)(c + d w), w^2 = -5
    return (p[0]*q[0] - 5*p[1]*q[1], p[0]*q[1] + p[1]*q[0])
def egcd(a, b):
    if b == 0: return (abs(a), (1 if a >= 0 else -1), 0)
    g, x, y = egcd(b, a % b); return (g, y, x - (a // b) * y)
def lattice(gens):  # Z-span of g and g*w for ideal generators g
    vs = []
    for g in gens: vs += [g, mul(g, (0, 1))]
    # basis {(h,0), (c,e)}: e = gcd of second coords
    e = 0; u = (0, 0)
    for v in vs:
        if v[1] == 0: continue
        if e == 0: e, u = abs(v[1]), (v if v[1] > 0 else (-v[0], -v[1])); continue
        g, s, t = egcd(e, v[1]); u = (s*u[0] + t*v[0], s*u[1] + t*v[1]); e = g
    h = 0
    for v in vs + [mul(u, (0, 1))]:
        if e: k = v[1] // e; w0 = v[0] - k*u[0]
        else: w0 = v[0]
        h = gcd(h, w0)
    return (h, e, u[0] % h if h else u[0])
def prod(I, J): return [mul(a, b) for a in I for b in J]
assert mul((1, 1), (1, -1)) == (6, 0)
P2 = [(2, 0), (1, 1)]; P3p = [(3, 0), (1, -1)]
assert lattice(prod(P2, P2)) == lattice([(2, 0)])
assert lattice(prod(P2, P3p)) == lattice([(1, -1)])
assert lattice(P2) == (2, 1, 1)  # P2 = {a + b w : a = b mod 2}, index 2
assert (3 - 0) % 2 == 1  # 3 = 3 + 0w has a - b odd, so 3 not in P2

checks.python:
import random, sympy as sp
def mul(p, q):
    a, b = p; c, d = q
    return (a*c - 5*b*d, a*d + b*c)
chi = lambda p: (p[0] + p[1]) % 3
random.seed(1)
for _ in range(2000):
    p = (random.randint(-50, 50), random.randint(-50, 50)); q = (random.randint(-50, 50), random.randint(-50, 50))
    assert chi(mul(p, q)) == (chi(p) * chi(q)) % 3
    s = (p[0] + q[0], p[1] + q[1]); assert chi(s) == (chi(p) + chi(q)) % 3
assert chi((1, 1)) == 2 and chi((1, -1)) == 0 and chi((3, 0)) == 0 and chi((6, 0)) == 0
assert mul((1, 1), (1, -1)) == (6, 0)
w = sp.sqrt(-5)
assert sp.simplify(1/(1+w) - (1-w)/6) == 0
# kernel generated by 3 and 1-w: a+bw = (a+b) - b(1-w)
for a in range(-6, 7):
    for b in range(-6, 7):
        t = mul((-b, 0), (1, -1))                 # -b(1 - w)
        assert (a + b + t[0], t[1]) == (a, b)     # a + b w = (a+b) - b(1-w)
        if (a + b) % 3 == 0: assert chi((a, b)) == 0
